1.1.title: Topic 1.1 · Elements, Minerals and Rocks
1.1.spec: Elements in minerals, crystal structures, diagnostic properties, rock classification

sections.heading: Mineral Definition & Bonding
points: Mineral definition: A naturally occurring, inorganic crystalline solid with a definite chemical composition and ordered internal atomic structure.
Silicate Tetrahedron [SiO4]4-: Fundamental building block. 1 silicon ion surrounded by 4 oxygen ions in tetrahedral coordination.

Bond types: Covalent (strong, directional, e.g. diamond/quartz), Ionic (transfer of electrons, moderate strength, e.g. halite), Metallic (electron sea, high conductivity, e.g. pyrite), van der Waals (weak intermolecular, cleavage planes in graphite/mica).

sections.heading: Silicate Frameworks & Cleavage Rules
points: Isolated tetrahedra: Olivine (Mg,Fe)2SiO4. No cleavage, fracture only. High density.
Single chains: Augite / Pyroxene. Chains bonded by cations. Two cleavage planes intersecting at 90° (87°/93°).
Double chains: Hornblende / Amphibole. Two cleavage planes intersecting at 60° and 120° (56°/124°).
Sheet silicates: Micas (Biotite / Muscovite). Tetrahedra share 3 oxygens. One perfect basal cleavage.
3D Framework: Quartz (SiO2) - shares all 4 oxygens, no cleavage, conchoidal fracture. Feldspars (Orthoclase / Plagioclase) - 2 cleavages at ~90°.

sections.heading: Diagnostic Properties (Hand Specimen & Thin Section)
points: Hardness (Mohs scale): Talc(1) < Gypsum(2) < [Fingernail ~2.5] < Calcite(3) < [Copper ~3.5] < Fluorite(4) < Apatite(5) < [Steel/Glass ~5.5] < Orthoclase(6) < Quartz(7) < Topaz(8) < Corundum(9) < Diamond(10).

Calcite vs Quartz: Calcite scratches with copper/nail (H=3), effervesces with dilute cold HCl (CaCO3 + 2HCl -> CaCl2 + H2O + CO2), 3 directions of rhombohedral cleavage. Quartz scratches glass (H=7), no acid reaction, conchoidal fracture.
Thin section optical properties:
• Plane polarised light (PPL): Relief (refractive index vs resin), Pleochroism (colour change on rotation e.g. Biotite brown-yellow, Hornblende green-brown), Cleavage traces.

• Crossed polars (XPL): Birefringence / Interference colours (order of colours on Michel-Lévy chart), Extinction angle (straight/parallel in quartz/orthoclase/biotite, inclined in augite/hornblende), Twinning (cross-hatched in microcline, albite polysynthetic stripes in plagioclase, Carlsbad simple twin in orthoclase).

sections.heading: Goldich Weathering Series & Stability
points: Minerals that crystallise at the highest temperatures and pressures (least like surface conditions) weather the fastest.
Susceptibility to chemical weathering: Olivine (fastest) > Augite > Hornblende > Biotite > Plagioclase > Orthoclase > Muscovite > Quartz (most resistant).
Quartz and clays dominate mature sedimentary deposits because quartz is mechanically hard and chemically inert.

2.1.title: Topic 2.1 · Sedimentary Rocks & Surface Processes
2.1.spec: Weathering, transport, deposition, textures, clastic/chemical rocks, diagenesis

sections.heading: Weathering & Transport
points: Mechanical weathering: Freeze-thaw (9% water expansion in joints), Exfoliation / onion-skin (insolation thermal expansion/contraction in arid climates), Salt crystallisation.
Chemical weathering:
• Carbonation: Rainwater dissolves CO2 -> carbonic acid (H2CO3) dissolving limestone.
• Hydrolysis: Acidified water attacks feldspar -> kaolinite (china clay) + silicic acid + soluble K+/Na+ ions.
• Oxidation: Iron minerals (e.g. olivine, augite, pyrite) react with oxygen -> hematite / limonite (rust red).
Hjulström Curve: Relates sediment grain size to water flow velocity required for erosion (entrainment), transport, and deposition.
• Clay/silt requires higher velocity to entrain than sand due to electrostatic cohesion.
• Sand entrains at the lowest velocity (~20 cm/s).
• Deposition occurs whenever velocity drops below settling velocity.

sections.heading: Textural Maturity & Clastic Classification
points: Grain size (Wentworth scale): Gravel / Rudaceous (>2 mm), Sand / Arenaceous (0.0625 mm - 2 mm), Mud / Argillaceous (<0.0625 mm, silt and clay).
Textural maturity: Increases with transport distance and time: Poorly sorted + angular + high matrix -> Well sorted + well rounded + low matrix (orthoquartzite).
Clastic rock types:
• Breccia: Angular clasts (>2 mm), near-source deposit (scree / fault talus / wadi flash flood).
• Conglomerate: Rounded clasts (>2 mm), high-energy aqueous transport (beach / high-energy river channel).
• Orthoquartzite: >95% quartz grains, well rounded, well sorted, silica cement; high-energy shallow marine / beach.
• Arkose: >25% feldspar, pink/red, moderate sorting/rounding; rapid deposition from granitic source in semi-arid alluvial fan.
• Greywacke: Poorly sorted, angular grains in dark fine-grained muddy matrix (>15%); submarine turbidity current deposit.

sections.heading: Sedimentary Structures & Way-Up Criteria
points: Cross-bedding: Formed by migrating ripples/dunes. Asymptotic curve at base, sharp truncation at top by erosion. Way-up: Tops truncated. Paleocurrent: Dips down-current.
Graded bedding: Coarse clasts at base fining upward into fine silt/mud (density current / turbidity current settling). Way-up: Coarse at base, fine at top.
Asymmetrical ripples: Formed by unidirectional current (river, wind); steep lee slope down-current.
Symmetrical ripples: Formed by bidirectional oscillatory wave action in shallow water; sharp crests point up.
Desiccation mudcracks: V-shaped cracks in mud due to subaerial drying; V points downwards.

sections.heading: Carbonate & Chemical Sediments & Diagenesis
points: Oolitic limestone: Formed of spherical ooids (calcite precipitated concentrically around nucleus in warm, agitated, supersaturated shallow marine water).
Bioclastic limestone: Abundant fossil fragments (crinoids, bivalves, corals) cemented by sparry calcite.
Chalk: Pure white micrite of microscopic coccolith plates (calcareous nannoplankton) in quiet pelagic marine shelf.
Evaporites: Halite (NaCl), Gypsum (CaSO4·2H2O), Anhydrite. Sequential precipitation in restricted marine basins with high evaporation > precipitation.
Diagenesis stages:
1. Compaction: Expulsion of pore water, reduction of porosity.
2. Cementation: Precipitation of mineral matter (calcite, quartz, iron oxide) from pore fluids, binding grains.
3. Recrystallisation / Neomorphism: Unstable aragonite converts to stable calcite.

2.2.title: Topic 2.2 · Igneous & Metamorphic Rocks
2.2.spec: Magma chemistry, cooling textures, intrusions/extrusions, contact/regional metamorphism

sections.heading: Magma Compositions & Igneous Classification
points: Basaltic / Mafic (45–52% SiO2): Low viscosity, high temp (1000–1200°C), dense, low gas. Minerals: Ca-rich plagioclase, augite, olivine. Extrusive: Basalt. Intrusive: Gabbro / Dolerite.
Andesitic / Intermediate (52–66% SiO2): Moderate viscosity & temp (800–1000°C). Minerals: Na-Ca plagioclase, hornblende, biotite. Extrusive: Andesite. Intrusive: Diorite.

Rhyolitic / Silicic / Felsic (>66% SiO2): High viscosity, lower temp (700–900°C), low density, volatile-rich (explosive). Minerals: Quartz, orthoclase, Na-plagioclase, muscovite/biotite. Extrusive: Rhyolite. Intrusive: Granite.

sections.heading: Igneous Textures & Cooling Rates
points: Equigranular / Phaneritic: Coarse crystals (>1 mm), uniform slow cooling deep underground (e.g. granite, gabbro).
Aphanitic: Fine crystals (<1 mm), rapid cooling at or near surface (e.g. basalt, rhyolite).
Porphyritic: Two distinct crystal sizes: large phenocrysts formed during early slow cooling at depth, set in fine groundmass formed during rapid cooling upon ascent/eruption.
Glassy (Obsidian): Instantaneous quenching, no time for crystal lattice to form.
Vesicular & Amygdaloidal: Gas bubbles trapped upon eruption (vesicles e.g. pumice, scoria); later filled by secondary minerals like calcite or quartz (amygdales).

sections.heading: Intrusions vs Extrusions (Field Recognition)
points: Concordant intrusions: Parallel to bedding. Sill: Chilled margins top and bottom; baked margins top and bottom; country rock xenoliths; no vesicles.
Extrusive lava flow: Chilled margin only at base; baked margin only below; vesicular, weathered/eroded top; fragments incorporated into overlying sedimentary bed.
Discordant intrusions: Cut across country rock. Dyke (steep tabular sheet), Pluton / Batholith (large discordant magma chamber >100 km²).

sections.heading: Contact (Thermal) Metamorphism
points: High temperature, low pressure, isotropic (uniform) confining stress. Occurs in metamorphic aureole surrounding igneous intrusions.
Aureole zones in pelitic (shale/mudstone) host rock:
• Outer zone (lowest temp): Spotted slate / Spotted rock (incipient growth of biotite/cordierite clusters).
• Middle zone: Andalusite hornfels (porphyroblasts of chiastolite with carbonaceous cross inclusions).
• Inner zone (highest temp): Sillimanite-cordierite hornfels (dense, hard, granoblastic, non-foliated).
Pure rocks: Limestone -> Marble (coarse granoblastic calcite); Sandstone -> Metaquartzite (interlocking quartz grains).

sections.heading: Regional Metamorphism & Foliation Sequence
points: High directed stress + high confining pressure + elevated temperature. Convergent plate collisions / orogenesis.
Barrovian prograde metamorphic zones (pelite sequence):
1. Slate: Microscopic platy minerals aligned perpendicular to maximum principal stress (\(\sigma_1\)) -> slaty cleavage.
2. Phyllite: Fine white mica/chlorite gives a silky lustrous sheen; wavy foliation.
3. Schist: Medium-coarse visible platy minerals (muscovite/biotite) forming continuous foliation (schistosity); contains porphyroblasts (garnet, staurolite).
4. Gneiss: High-grade segregation into alternating light quartzo-feldspathic bands and dark mafic (biotite/hornblende) bands (gneissose banding).
5. Migmatite: Partial melting of felsic components (anatexis) forming mixed metamorphic-igneous rock.

2.3.title: Topic 2.3 · Deformation, Folds, Faults & Maps
2.3.spec: Stress/strain, strike/dip, fold classification, fault types and evidence, unconformities, geological map interpretation

sections.heading: Stress, Strain & Orientation
points: Strike: The compass trend of a horizontal line on a dipping planar surface (e.g. 045°).
Dip: The maximum angle of inclination measured perpendicular to strike downwards from the horizontal (e.g. 30° SE).
Apparent dip: The inclination measured in any non-perpendicular direction to strike; always less than true dip.
Brittle vs Ductile deformation: Low temp/confining pressure + fast strain rate = brittle (faults/joints); High temp/pressure + slow strain rate = ductile (folding/ductile shear).

sections.heading: Fold Classification & Geometry
points: Anticline: Convex upwards fold with oldest strata in core.
Syncline: Concave upwards fold with youngest strata in core.
Symmetrical fold: Axial plane is vertical; limbs dip in opposite directions at equal angles.
Asymmetrical fold: Axial plane is inclined; limbs dip at different angles.
Overturned fold: One limb is tilted beyond vertical so strata are inverted (younger below older).
Recumbent fold: Axial plane is horizontal or sub-horizontal (dip <10°).

Plunging fold: Fold hinge line is inclined to the horizontal; produces V-shaped or U-shaped outcrop pattern on flat terrain. Anticlines plunge towards the closed apex of the V; synclines plunge towards the open end.

sections.heading: Fault Mechanics & Identification
points: Normal fault: Extensional stress (\(\sigma_1\) vertical). Hanging wall moves down relative to footwall. Lengthens crust. Omits strata on maps.
Reverse fault: Compressional stress (\(\sigma_1\) horizontal). Hanging wall moves up relative to footwall (dip >45°). Shortens crust. Duplicates strata.
Thrust fault: Low-angle reverse fault (dip <45°); places older rocks over younger rocks over large lateral distances.
Strike-slip (tear) fault: Shear stress (\(\sigma_2\) vertical). Lateral displacement (dextral = clockwise/right-lateral; sinistral = anticlockwise/left-lateral).

Field & map evidence for faulting: Truncation and offset of beds, slickensides (grooves showing movement direction), fault breccia / fault gouge, drag folds (limbs flexed towards fault movement), spring lines.

sections.heading: Unconformities & The Rule of V's
points: Angular unconformity: Gap in geological record where tilted/folded older rocks are eroded and overlain by flatter younger rocks.
• Evidence: Truncation of beds below, dip discordance, basal conglomerate containing pebbles derived from underlying unit.
Rule of V's (Map Outcrop Pattern across Valleys):
• Horizontal beds: Contour parallel; outcrop bands follow contours.
• Vertical beds: Straight lines across topography regardless of valleys/hills.
• Dipping beds: V points in the direction of dip down a valley, UNLESS the bed dips downstream at a lower angle than the valley gradient.

3.1.title: Topic 3.1 · Present-Day Processes & Fossils
3.1.spec: Fossil preservation, taphonomy, life vs death assemblages, morphological features & paleoecology

sections.heading: Fossil Preservation & Taphonomy
points: Fossil: Any preserved remains, impression, or trace of organisms from past geological ages.

Favourable preservation factors: Hard skeleton/shell (calcite, silica, apatite), rapid burial (prevents scavenging and mechanical destruction), low energy environment, anoxic bottom waters (inhibits bacterial decay).
Preservation modes:
• Replacement / Petrifaction: Original mineral replaced molecule by molecule (e.g. pyritisation, silicification).
• Recrystallisation: Unstable aragonite converts to coarse calcite crystals.
• Moulds & Casts: Shell dissolves leaving external mould (impressing wall) and internal mould (steinkern); infilled with sediment/mineral = cast.
• Carbonisation: Volatiles expelled leaving thin black carbon film (plants, graptolites).
• Trace fossils (ichnofossils): Tracks, trails, burrows, coprolites, borings; classify behavior (feeding, dwelling, resting, locomotion).

sections.heading: Life Assemblage vs Death Assemblage
points: Life Assemblage (In Situ / Biocoenosis):
• Organisms preserved in living position (e.g. upright corals, bivalves in burrows).
• Articulated multi-part skeletons (complete trilobites with free cheeks attached; bivalves with valves closed).
• Wide size distribution / growth stages (juveniles and adults together).
• Unbroken, unworn delicate spines/frills preserved.
Death Assemblage (Transported / Thanatocoenosis):
• Disarticulated valves/segments (isolated bivalve valves, separated trilobite cranidia/pygidia).
• Hydrodynamically sorted (all shells same size/weight).
• Broken, abraded, rounded shell fragments.
• Current alignment of elongate fossils (graptolites, belemnites, tentaculites).

sections.heading: Key Fossil Groups & Paleoecological Morphologies
points: Trilobites (Arthropods, Cambrian–Permian): Cephalon (head), thorax (segmented), pygidium (tail). Glabella, compound eyes, facial sutures. Pelagic/swimmer (huge eyes, streamlined), Benthic crawler (medium eyes, sturdy legs), Burrower (no eyes, spade-shaped cephalon).

Brachiopods (Cambrian–Recent): Bilateral symmetry perpendicular to hinge line (plane cuts through middle of both valves). Pedicle valve larger with pedicle foramen (anchored to sea floor), brachial valve supports lophophore filter-feeding organ.

Bivalves (Molluscs, Cambrian–Recent): Bilateral symmetry between the two valves (valves are mirror images of each other). Pallial sinus presence = deep burrower with retractable siphons; thick ribbed shell = high energy shallow marine.

Corals (Cnidarians): Calcareous skeleton (corallite), septa (radiating radial plates), tabulae (horizontal floor plates). Solitary (horn corals e.g. Zaphrentis) vs colonial. Shallow, warm (>20°C), clear, agitated, normal marine salinity reef environments.

Graptolites (Hemichordates, Cambrian–Devonian): Planktonic colonial organisms. Stipes composed of thecae housing zooids. Rapid morphological evolution: Ordovician multi-stiped pendent/horizontal -> Silurian single-stiped scandent (Monograptus). Excellent zone fossils for deep marine shales.

3.2.title: Topic 3.2 · Relative & Absolute Time
3.2.spec: Principles of stratigraphy, way-up criteria, zone fossils, radiometric decay, geological timescale

sections.heading: Principles of Relative Dating
points: Law of Superposition: In undeformed sedimentary/volcanic sequence, oldest bed at bottom, youngest at top.
Principle of Original Horizontality: Sediments are deposited under gravity in flat, horizontal layers; tilting/folding occurred post-deposition.
Cross-cutting relationships: Any feature (fault, igneous intrusion, mineral vein, unconformity) that cuts across another rock unit is younger than the rock it cuts.
Principle of Inclusions: Fragments (xenoliths in igneous rocks; pebbles in conglomerates) are always older than the rock containing them.

sections.heading: Way-Up Evidence (Top/Bottom Criteria)
points: Sedimentary way-up: Cross-bedding truncation (eroded at top), Graded bedding (coarse at bottom, fine at top), Ripple crests (point up), Mudcracks (V points down), Flute casts/load casts (bulbous downward projections on bed base).
Volcanic way-up: Pillow lavas (convex rounded top, cusped/keeled base fitting into underlying pillow), baked margin on bottom of flow only, vesicular zone at flow top.
Paleontological way-up: Plant roots branching downwards; corals growing upright.

sections.heading: Biostratigraphy & Ideal Zone Fossils
points: Characteristics of an ideal Index / Zone Fossil:
1. Rapid evolution: Short stratigraphic range (precise dating).
2. Geographically widespread: Found across basins and continents.
3. Abundant: Easily found in rock exposures and drill cores.
4. Easily identifiable: Distinct morphological features.
5. Facies-independent: Pelagic / planktonic (floated in water column, found in many sediment types).
Best index fossils: Graptolites (Ordovician–Silurian), Ammonites (Devonian–Cretaceous), Microfossils/Conodonts/Foraminifera (Phanerozoic).

sections.heading: Radiometric Absolute Dating
points: Radioactive decay: Unstable parent isotope decays to stable radiogenic daughter isotope at a constant exponential rate unaffected by heat, pressure, or chemistry.
Half-life (t1/2): Time taken for half the radioactive parent atoms to decay.

Closure temperature: The temperature below which isotopes can no longer diffuse out of the crystal lattice. If rock is reheated during metamorphism above closure temp, radiogenic daughter escapes and radiometric clock is reset.
Key isotope systems:
• K-Ar / Ar-Ar: K-40 decays to Ar-40 (t1/2 = 1.25 Ga). Dating igneous/metamorphic biotite, hornblende, sanidine.
• U-Pb: U-238/U-235 in Zircon. Zircon has very high closure temp (>900°C), retains primary crystallisation age.
• Carbon-14: t1/2 = 5,730 yrs. Only dates organic material up to ~50,000 years (Quaternary).

4.1.title: Topic 4.1 · Earth Structure & Seismology
4.1.spec: Seismic body waves, refraction/reflection, Earth's internal layers, shadow zones, isostasy

sections.heading: Seismic Waves & Propagation
points: P-waves (Primary / Compressional): Longitudinal particle motion parallel to wave propagation. Travel through solids and liquids. Fastest wave (~6–13 km/s).

S-waves (Secondary / Shear): Transverse particle motion perpendicular to wave propagation. Shear elastic resistance only. Cannot travel through liquids or gases (velocity drops to zero). Slower than P-waves (~3.5–7 km/s).
Ray Paths & Velocity: In a homogeneous solid, velocity increases with depth due to rising rigidity and incompressibility exceeding density increase -> seismic rays refract/bend upwards.

sections.heading: Earth's Internal Discontinuities & Layers
points: Moho (Mohorovičić Discontinuity): Crust-mantle boundary. P-wave velocity jumps abruptly from ~6.0 km/s (crust) to ~8.0 km/s (peridotite mantle).
• Continental crust: 30–70 km thick, granitic/felsic, density ~2.7 g/cm³.
• Oceanic crust: 5–10 km thick, basaltic/gabbroic, density ~3.0 g/cm³.
Low Velocity Zone (LVZ / Asthenosphere): Depth 100–250 km. P and S velocities dip slightly due to 1–2% partial melting; ductile, allows tectonic plate movement.
Gutenberg Discontinuity (Core-Mantle Boundary / CMB, 2900 km):
• P-wave velocity drops sharply from ~13.7 km/s to ~8.1 km/s.
• S-wave velocity drops to zero -> proves the outer core is liquid.
Lehmann Discontinuity (Inner Core Boundary, 5150 km): P-wave velocity jumps from ~10.3 km/s to ~11.2 km/s -> confirms solid inner core (high pressure prevents melting).

sections.heading: Seismic Shadow Zones
points: P-wave shadow zone (103° to 142°): Caused by severe refraction (bending inwards) of P-waves entering the slower liquid outer core at the Gutenberg discontinuity.
S-wave shadow zone (103° to 180°): Complete absence of direct S-waves beyond 103° on either side of earthquake focus because S-waves cannot travel through the liquid outer core.

sections.heading: Isostasy & Gravity
points: Isostasy: Gravitational equilibrium between Earth's lithosphere floating on the denser asthenosphere.
Airy hypothesis: Uniform crustal density, varying root depth (tall mountains have deep buoyant crustal roots).
Post-glacial rebound: Melting of continental ice sheets causes lithosphere to slowly uplift as asthenosphere flows back in.

4.2.title: Topic 4.2 · Global Tectonics
4.2.spec: Continental drift, paleomagnetism, plate boundaries, driving forces, mantle plumes

sections.heading: Continental Drift & Paleomagnetism
points: Evidence for drift: Continental shelf jigsaw fit, matching fossil distributions (Glossopteris flora, Mesosaurus), matching mountain belts across Atlantic, late Paleozoic glacial striations and tillites across southern continents (Gondwana).
Remanent Magnetism: As mafic lava cools below the Curie point of magnetite (~580°C), magnetic dipoles align with Earth's current magnetic field and lock in.

Seafloor Spreading (Vine-Matthews-Morley): Symmetrical marine magnetic anomalies ('stripes' of normal and reversed polarities) parallel to mid-ocean ridges. Ocean crust age increases symmetrically away from ridge axis.

sections.heading: Plate Boundaries & Characteristic Features
points: Divergent (Constructive): Decompression melting of asthenospheric mantle -> basaltic volcanism, pillow lavas, sheeted dykes, normal fault grabens, shallow earthquakes (e.g. Mid-Atlantic Ridge, East African Rift).
Convergent (Destructive) - Ocean/Continent (Andean):
• Subducting slab creates deep ocean trench and Benioff zone (earthquakes from shallow to deep down to 700 km).
• Flux melting (water released by dehydration of slab lowers mantle solidus) produces intermediate andesitic/dacitic arc volcanism.
• Accretionary wedge of scraped-off sediments.
Convergent - Continent/Continent (Himalayan): Intense crustal shortening, folding, reverse/thrust faults, regional metamorphism, high mountain plateau, no volcanism, shallow/intermediate earthquakes.
Conservative / Transform: Lateral displacement, strike-slip faulting, shallow earthquakes, no volcanism (e.g. San Andreas Fault).

sections.heading: Plate Driving Forces
points: Slab Pull: Cold, dense, subducted oceanic lithosphere undergoes eclogite metamorphism (very dense), sinking into asthenosphere under gravity and pulling the rest of the plate behind it. Dominant driving force (>90%).
Ridge Push: Gravitational sliding of elevated, buoyant newly formed oceanic crust at mid-ocean ridge downslope away from the ridge axis.
Basal Drag: Minor traction from mantle convection currents dragging base of lithospheric plate.

sections.heading: Hotspots & Mantle Plumes
points: Stationary thermal upwellings originating from core-mantle boundary (D'' layer).
As tectonic plate moves over the fixed hotspot, a linear chain of volcanoes forms with progressive age increase away from the active volcanic centre (e.g. Hawaiian-Emperor seamount chain).
Direction of plate motion is towards the oldest volcano; rate of plate motion = distance / age difference.

G1.1.title: Topic G1.1 · Magma Generation & Evolution
G1.1.spec: Partial melting, magmatic differentiation, phase diagrams, crystallization paths

sections.heading: Magma Generation Mechanisms
points: Decompression melting: Upward movement of solid mantle peridotite without loss of heat (adiabatic) crosses solidus. Occurs at mid-ocean ridges and hotspots.

Flux melting (hydration): Subducting oceanic slab dewaters (serpentinite/clays break down); water enters overlying mantle wedge, lowering solidus temperature below ambient temperature. Occurs at subduction zones.
Thermal melting: Conductive heat transfer from hot basaltic magma underplating crust melts continental crust.

sections.heading: Magmatic Differentiation Processes
points: Fractional crystallisation / Crystal settling: Early-formed dense mafic minerals (olivine, Ca-plagioclase, pyroxene) settle out of liquid under gravity, depleting magma in Mg, Fe, Ca and enriching remaining liquid in Si, Na, K.
Crustal assimilation: Hot rising magma melts and incorporates wall rock (xenolith digestion), shifting magma towards more silicic composition.
Magma mixing: Influx of primitive mafic magma into evolving silicic chamber creates intermediate hybrids with mixed phenocrysts (e.g. resorbed quartz beside calcic plagioclase).
Liquid immiscibility: Magma splits into two unmixable liquids (e.g. sulfide-rich melt and silicate-rich melt).

sections.heading: Phase Diagrams & The Lever Rule
points: Binary Eutectic System (e.g. Diopside-Anorthite):
• Liquidus: Curve above which system is completely liquid.
• Solidus: Line below which system is completely solid.
• Eutectic point: Minimum melting temperature where liquid and both solid phases coexist at equilibrium. Final liquid always crystallises at eutectic composition.
Lever Rule calculation: Ratio of solid to liquid at any temperature: \(\% ext{Solid} = rac{ ext{Distance to Liquidus}}{ ext{Total tie-line width}} imes 100\).

G1.2.title: Topic G1.2 · Metamorphic Rocks: Mineralogy & Texture
G1.2.spec: Metamorphic facies, P-T-t paths, microstructures, porphyroblasts, shear zones

sections.heading: Metamorphic Facies & Tectonic Settings
points: Zeolite & Prehnite-Pumpellyite: Low P, low T; burial metamorphism.
Greenschist: Moderate P, moderate T (300–450°C). Key minerals: Chlorite, actinolite, albite, epidote.
Amphibolite: Moderate-high P, high T (500–700°C). Key minerals: Hornblende, plagioclase, garnet, staurolite.
Granulite: High T (>750°C), anhydrous, deep continental crust. Key minerals: Pyroxene, sillimanite, garnet, perthitic feldspar.
Blueschist: High P, low T. Subducting slab at ocean trenches. Key diagnostic mineral: Glaucophane (blue sodic amphibole).
Eclogite: Ultra-high P, high T. Deeply subducted crust. Key minerals: Omphacite (green sodic pyroxene) + Pyrope garnet (pink).

sections.heading: Microtextures & Shear-Sense Indicators
points: Porphyroblastic & Poikiloblastic: Large metamorphic crystals (e.g. garnet, staurolite, andalusite) containing inclusions of earlier matrix minerals (sieve texture).
Helicitic / Snowball Garnet: Sigmoidal spiral trails of quartz inclusions inside garnet prove crystal rotated during ductile shear (syn-tectonic growth).
Mylonites: Intense ductile grain-size reduction in shear zones. Features: Ribbon quartz, dynamically recrystallised mortar texture.
Rotated Porphyroclasts:
• Sigma (\(\sigma\)) clasts: Tails / wings extend symmetrically into foliation; indicate shear sense.
• Delta (\(\delta\)) clasts: Tails curved and wrapped around porphyroclast from significant rotation.

G1.3.title: Topic G1.3 · Sedimentary Modelling & Facies
G1.3.spec: Bouma sequence, turbidity currents, sequence stratigraphy, paleocurrent vectors

sections.heading: Bouma Sequence (Turbidite Deposition)
points: Formed by decelerating subaqueous density flow in deep marine environment.
Ta division: Massive to normally graded coarse sandstone/gravel, sharp erosive base with sole marks (flute casts, groove casts).
Tb division: Parallel plane-laminated sandstone (upper flow regime flat bed).
Tc division: Ripple cross-laminated or climbing ripple sandstone/siltstone with convolute lamination (lower flow regime).
Td division: Parallel laminated siltstone.
Te division: Structureless hemipelagic clay/mud.

sections.heading: Paleocurrent Vector Mean & Distributions
points: Paleocurrent measurements: Flute casts, cross-bed dips, ripple crests, parting lineations.
• Unimodal distribution (rose diagram with one strong direction): Fluvial / river channel or delta.
• Bimodal / bipolar distribution (two opposite peaks 180° apart): Tidal marine shelf (flood and ebb tides).
• Polymodal / random: Deep ocean pelagic or aeolian variable dune.

G2.title: Topic G2 · Rock Deformation & Structures
G2.spec: Stress/strain ellipsoids, Flinn diagrams, deformation mechanisms, stereonets

sections.heading: Stress & Strain Ellipsoids
points: Stress: Force applied per unit area. Three mutually perpendicular principal stress axes: \(\sigma_1\) (maximum), \(\sigma_2\) (intermediate), \(\sigma_3\) (minimum).
Strain: Deformation/distortion of rock body resulting from applied stress. Strain ellipsoid axes: \(X \ge Y \ge Z\).
Flinn Diagram: Plots strain ratio \(a = X/Y\) vs \(b = Y/Z\).
• \(k > 1\): Constrictional strain (prolate 'cigar' shape, e.g. pencil cleavage).
• \(k = 1\): Plane strain (no volume change in Y).
• \(k < 1\): Flattening strain (oblate 'pancake' shape, e.g. slaty cleavage).

sections.heading: Deformation Mechanisms & Stereonets
points: Pressure solution: Dissolution of minerals at high-stress grain contacts and precipitation in low-stress shadows (forms stylolites in limestones).
Dislocation creep / Plastic glide: Movement of crystal lattice imperfections; dynamic recrystallisation.
Stereonet interpretation: Poles to bedding planes plotted on equal-area stereonet lie along a great circle (the \(\pi\)-girdle); the pole to this girdle defines the trend and plunge of the fold axis.

G3.1.title: Topic G3.1 · Fossils & Diversity of Life
G3.1.spec: Evolutionary rates, adaptive radiation, the Big Five mass extinctions, extinction triggers

sections.heading: Evolutionary Mechanisms & Patterns
points: Phyletic gradualism: Slow, steady, continuous transformation of lineages over geological time.
Punctuated equilibrium: Long periods of morphological stasis interrupted by rapid speciation events in small isolated populations.
Adaptive radiation: Rapid diversification of an ancestral group into many ecological niches following evolutionary novelty or mass extinction opening up vacant ecospace.

sections.heading: The Big Five Mass Extinctions
points: 1. End-Ordovician (~444 Ma): Glaciation on Gondwana, eustatic sea-level drop, loss of shallow marine shelf habitat.
2. Late Devonian (~375 Ma): Oceanic anoxia, cooling; hit shallow benthic corals/brachiopods.
3. End-Permian ('The Great Dying', ~252 Ma): Largest extinction in history (~96% marine species, ~70% terrestrial vertebrates lost).
• Causes: Siberian Traps flood basalt volcanism releasing massive CO2 and SO2 -> global warming, ocean acidification, widespread marine anoxia, ozone layer destruction.
4. End-Triassic (~201 Ma): Central Atlantic Magmatic Province (CAMP) rifting; paved way for dinosaur dominance.
5. End-Cretaceous (K-Pg, ~66 Ma): Non-avian dinosaurs, ammonites, marine reptiles extinct.
• Causes: Chicxulub bolide impact (Iridium anomaly in boundary clay, shocked quartz, tektites/microkrystites, tsunami deposits) combined with Deccan Traps volcanism.

G3.2.title: Topic G3.2 · Factors in Climate Change
G3.2.spec: Milankovitch cycles, greenhouse gases, plate tectonics, oceanic circulation

sections.heading: Milankovitch Astronomical Cycles
points: Orbital Eccentricity (100,000 & 400,000 yr): Earth's orbit cycles between circular and elliptical, altering total incoming solar radiation.

Obliquity / Axial Tilt (41,000 yr): Tilt cycles between 22.1° and 24.5° (currently 23.4°). Greater tilt = more extreme seasons (warmer summers, colder winters). Less tilt favours ice sheet growth as mild summers fail to melt winter snow.
Precession of Equinoxes (21,000–26,000 yr): Wobble of Earth's rotational axis; alters timing of seasons relative to perihelion.

sections.heading: Tectonic & Greenhouse Controls
points: Continental position: Landmasses over poles allow ice sheet buildup (e.g. Antarctica in Cenozoic).
Oceanic gateways: Opening of Drake Passage separated South America from Antarctica -> Antarctic Circumpolar Current thermally isolated Antarctica, initiating continental glaciation (~34 Ma).
Mountain uplift & CO2 drawdown: Himalayan collision exposed vast silicate rocks; intense chemical weathering (hydrolysis) drew down atmospheric CO2, driving global Cenozoic cooling.

G3.3.title: Topic G3.3 · Evidence for Climate Change
G3.3.spec: Oxygen isotope proxies (d18O), ice cores, sedimentary paleoclimate indicators

sections.heading: Oxygen Isotopes (d18O) as Paleothermometers
points: 16O (light) evaporates preferentially over 18O (heavy).
During Glacial / Icehouse Periods:
• Light 16O evaporates, falls as snow, and is trapped in continental ice sheets.
• Ice cores have negative \(\delta^{18} ext{O}\) (depleted in 18O).
• Oceans become enriched in 18O -> marine foraminifera shells have positive \(\delta^{18} ext{O}\).
During Interglacial Periods: Melting ice returns 16O to oceans; marine carbonate \(\delta^{18} ext{O}\) decreases.

sections.heading: Sedimentary & Biological Climate Indicators
points: Glacial: Tillites / diamictites (unsorted, striated clasts), dropstones deforming laminations in marine shale.
Arid / Desert: Aeolian dunes (large-scale cross-bedding), red beds (hematite coating), evaporites (halite, gypsum).
Humid / Tropical: Thick coal beds (warm swamps), laterites/bauxites (leached tropical soils).
Foraminiferal coiling: Neogloboquadrina pachyderma coils to the left (sinistral) in polar water (<7°C) and to the right (dextral) in warmer waters.

G4.1.title: Topic G4.1 · Concentration of Natural Resources
G4.1.spec: Magmatic, hydrothermal, placer, and residual ore formation

sections.heading: Magmatic & Hydrothermal Ore Deposits
points: Magmatic segregation / Immiscibility: Dense sulfide or oxide liquids separate from mafic magma and sink to base of intrusion (e.g. Bushveld chromite, Sudbury Ni-Cu).
Hydrothermal veins: Superheated volatile-rich aqueous fluids scavenge metals from cooling plutons and country rocks, precipitating ore minerals in fracture veins as pressure and temperature drop.
• Mineral zoning away from granite intrusion: Sn (cassiterite) & W (wolframite) closest (highest T) -> Cu (chalcopyrite) -> Zn (sphalerite) -> Pb (galena) -> Fe (pyrite) furthest.
Porphyry deposits: Massive low-grade copper/molybdenum deposits associated with subduction arc plutons; pervasive stockwork veinlet network.

sections.heading: Placer & Residual Deposits
points: Placer deposits: Mechanical concentration by fluvial/coastal currents.
• Requires minerals that are: Dense (high relative density), Chemically inert (resistant to weathering), and Mechanically hard (resist abrasion).
• Examples: Native Gold (RD 19.3), Diamond (H 10), Cassiterite (SnO2, RD 7.0), Magnetite, Zircon.
• Concentrated at inside of meander bends, downstream of confluences, behind rock bars, and plunge pools.
Residual deposits (Bauxite & Kaolinite):
• Bauxite (Al ore): Extreme tropical weathering leaches silica, leaving insoluble hydrous aluminium oxides (gibbsite).
• Kaolinite (China clay): Hydrothermal or deep weathering breakdown of feldspar in granites.

G4.2.title: Topic G4.2 · Oil, Gas & Coal Formation
G4.2.spec: Petroleum system elements, oil/gas windows, reservoir properties, coalification

sections.heading: The Petroleum System (Five Essentials)
points: 1. Source Rock: Organic-rich (sapropelic) marine mudstone/shale with >1% Total Organic Carbon (TOC). Plankton buried in anoxic conditions.
2. Maturation: Thermal cooking under burial:
• Oil Window: 60°C to 120°C (burial depth 2–4 km).
• Gas Window: 120°C to 200°C (burial depth 4–6 km).
• Above 200°C: Over-mature; hydrocarbons graphitised/destroyed.
3. Reservoir Rock: Porous (stores fluids) and permeable (allows extraction). E.g. well-sorted sandstone, oolitic/reefal limestone.
4. Cap Rock (Seal): Impermeable rock barrier preventing escape. E.g. thick shale, mudstone, or evaporites (halite/anhydrite).
5. Trap: Geometric arrangement halting migration:
• Structural: Anticlinal crest, fault trap (reservoir juxtaposed against impermeable shale), salt dome/diapir.
• Stratigraphic: Unconformity trap, sand pinch-out / lens, reef buildup.

sections.heading: Hydraulic Properties & Coal Series
points: Porosity: Volume of pore space as percentage of total rock volume: \(\phi = rac{V_{ ext{void}}}{V_{ ext{total}}} imes 100\).
Permeability: Interconnectedness of pores allowing fluid flow.
Coalification Rank: Progressive increase in burial T, P, and time:
• Peat -> Lignite (brown coal) -> Bituminous coal (lustrous, black) -> Anthracite (hard, shiny, non-smudge).
• Trend: Carbon content increases (up to 95%), calorific value increases, moisture and volatile content decrease.

G4.3.title: Topic G4.3 · Prospecting Techniques
G4.3.spec: Geophysical surveys (gravity, magnetic, seismic), geochemical sampling, borehole logging

sections.heading: Geophysical Exploration Methods
points: Gravity survey (Gravimeter): Measures local variations in gravitational field (\(g\)).
• Positive anomaly (gravity high): Dense subsurface bodies (massive metallic sulfide ore bodies, mafic/ultramafic intrusions).
• Negative anomaly (gravity low): Low-density bodies (salt domes, granite plutons, sedimentary basins, caverns).
Magnetic survey (Magnetometer): Detects variations in Earth's magnetic field due to magnetic minerals (magnetite, pyrrhotite).

Seismic reflection: Generates acoustic waves; reflected at boundaries between rocks of differing acoustic impedance (\(Z = ho imes v\)). Produces cross-sectional profiles of subsurface structures and traps.

sections.heading: Geochemical Prospecting & Borehole Logging
points: Geochemical survey: Systematically samples soil, stream sediments, or water to identify anomalous concentrations above regional background levels.
• Contour maps plotted with isolines (e.g. 50 ppm, 100 ppm Cu); highest values pinpoint upstream or upslope ore subcrop.
Borehole geophysical logging:
• Gamma log: Measures natural radioactivity. High gamma = shale/clay (rich in K-40); Low gamma = sandstone, limestone, evaporites.
• Resistivity log: High resistivity = hydrocarbons or fresh water; Low resistivity = saline formation water in pores.
• Sonic log: Measures seismic velocity to calculate porosity.

T1.title: Theme T1 · Geohazards & Engineering
T1.spec: Earthquake hazards, volcanic monitoring, slope stability, engineering geology

sections.heading: Seismic Hazards & Volcanic Monitoring
points: Earthquake hazards: Ground shaking, liquefaction (water-saturated unconsolidated sand behaves as liquid), landslides, tsunamis.
Volcanic prediction precursors:
• Harmonic volcanic tremor and shallow earthquake swarms (magma moving through conduits).
• Ground deformation: Tiltmeters, GPS, and satellite InSAR detect swelling / inflation of volcanic edifice.
• Gas emissions: Increasing SO2 and CO2 emission rates and ratios.
• Thermal anomalies: FLIR infrared imaging detects rising magma.

sections.heading: Slope Stability & Engineering Geology
points: Factor of Safety (\(F\)): \(F = rac{\sum ext{Resisting Forces}}{\sum ext{Driving Forces}}\). If \(F > 1\) slope is stable; \(F < 1\) failure occurs.
• Driving forces: Gravity component parallel to slope, slope surcharge (buildings).
• Resisting forces: Cohesion, friction across potential slip planes.
• Pore water pressure: Reduces effective normal stress across slip planes, triggering landslides.
Engineering mitigation: Horizontal drainage pipes (relieves pore pressure), rock bolts (pins beds together across dip), retaining walls with weep holes, gabion baskets, shotcrete.

T2.title: Theme T2 · Geological Maps & Fieldwork
T2.spec: Structural contours, three-point problems, cross-section construction, map interpretation

sections.heading: Three-Point Problems & Strike Lines
points: Strike lines (structural contours): Straight lines connecting points of equal elevation on a planar geological surface (bedding plane or fault).
• The direction of a strike line is the strike of the bed.
• Spacing between strike lines indicates dip: closer lines = steeper dip; wider lines = gentler dip.
Dip calculation from strike lines: \( an( ext{Dip}) = rac{ ext{Contour Interval}}{ ext{Horizontal Distance between strike lines}}\).

T3.title: Theme T3 · Quaternary Geology
T3.spec: Glacial erosion/deposition, periglacial landforms, Quaternary paleoclimates

sections.heading: Glacial & Periglacial Processes
points: Glacial erosional landforms: Corries/cirques with tarns, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, U-shaped glacial troughs, hanging valleys, roche moutonnées (smooth plucked stoss-and-lee).
Glacial depositional landforms: Moraines (terminal, lateral, medial, recessional), drumlins (streamlined elongate hills, steep blunt stoss end points up-ice), erratics, kettle holes.

Periglacial landforms: Permafrost and active layer; solifluction/gelifluction sheets; patterned ground (stone polygons sorted by frost heave); ice wedges and fossil ice wedge pseudomorphs (prove continuous permafrost).

T4.title: Theme T4 · Evolution of Britain
T4.spec: Terranes of Britain, Caledonian and Variscan orogenies, paleolatitude drift

sections.heading: Terranes & Orogenic Cycles of the British Isles
points: Caledonian Orogeny (Ordovician–Devonian): Closure of Iapetus Ocean; Laurentia (Scotland & NW Ireland) collided with Eastern Avalonia (England & Wales). Marked by the Iapetus Suture zone.
Variscan Orogeny (Carboniferous–Permian): Closure of Rheic Ocean; collision of Armorica/Gondwana with Euramerica to assemble Pangaea. Intense folding in SW England (Cornubian batholith emplacement).
Northward Drift of Britain:
• Cambrian: ~60°S (cold seas).
• Carboniferous: Equatorial ~0° (warm tropical coal-forming swamps).
• Permian–Triassic: 10°–20°N (arid trade wind desert, New Red Sandstone).
• Present: ~54°N (temperate).

T5.title: Theme T5 · Geology of the Lithosphere
T5.spec: Ophiolite suites, oceanic crust metamorphism, continental crust accretion

sections.heading: Ophiolite Complex (Oceanic Lithosphere Section)
points: Complete preserved section of oceanic crust and upper mantle obducted onto land.
1. Pelagic sediment: Deep-sea chert, black mudstone, siliceous ooze (top).
2. Pillow basalts: Extrusive lavas quenched in seawater.
3. Sheeted dyke complex: Sub-vertical feeder dykes formed in 100% extensional spreading zone.
4. Gabbro: Coarse-grained, isotropic at top, layered cumulate at base.
5. Moho Discontinuity: Petrographic boundary between gabbro and peridotite.
6. Ultramafic mantle: Harzburgite / lherzolite, often altered to serpentinite.
